title: Astrophysics & Cosmology
subject: Astrophysics
summary: Survey of how physics you already know (radiation, thermodynamics, quantum statistics, relativity) explains stars, galaxies, and the history of the universe: from starlight and stellar structure to compact objects, the Friedmann equations, the CMB, nucleosynthesis, dark matter and dark energy, and inflation.

units.title: Stellar observables and radiation
units.summary: How astronomers get distance, luminosity, temperature, and composition from starlight: parallax, magnitudes, Planck's law, and the Boltzmann and Saha equations (the same Boltzmann populations and ionization equilibria a chemist uses in spectroscopy).

lessons.title: Distances, magnitudes, and luminosity
objectives: Compute a stellar distance in parsecs from a parallax angle in arcseconds and convert between parsecs, light-years, and meters.
Convert between apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude, and distance using the distance modulus m - M = 5 log10(d/10 pc).
Use the inverse-square law F = L/(4 pi d^2) to compare the luminosities of two stars from their flux ratio or magnitude difference.
Explain why the magnitude scale is logarithmic and that a difference of 5 magnitudes is exactly a factor of 100 in flux.

lessons.title: Blackbody radiation, color, and temperature
objectives: State Planck's law and derive Wien's displacement law by locating the peak of B_lambda(T); recite the numerical constant.
Obtain the Stefan-Boltzmann law L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T_eff^4 from the integral of the Planck function and use it to find a star's radius from L and T_eff.
Explain how the B-V color index tracks temperature and why it is independent of distance.
Explain how Planck's energy quantization resolves the ultraviolet catastrophe and connect the same Planck distribution to lamp sources and thermal radiation in IR/UV spectroscopy.

lessons.title: Spectral lines, Boltzmann and Saha, and the HR diagram
objectives: Compute Balmer-series wavelengths from the Rydberg formula and explain absorption lines as bound-bound transitions.
Apply the Boltzmann equation to find the ratio of populations of two atomic levels at temperature T (the same factor that governs vibrational and electronic populations in molecular spectroscopy).
Apply the Saha equation as an ionization equilibrium (a gas-phase equilibrium constant) to explain why hydrogen Balmer lines are strongest near 10,000 K, not in the hottest stars.
Order the spectral classes O B A F G K M by temperature and place main-sequence stars, giants, and white dwarfs on the HR diagram using L, T, and R contours.

units.title: Stellar structure
units.summary: A star as a self-gravitating ball of gas in balance: hydrostatic equilibrium, the equation of state (ideal gas, radiation, degeneracy from P7), nuclear energy sources, and energy transport yield the main sequence.

lessons.title: Hydrostatic equilibrium and the virial theorem
objectives: Derive the equation of hydrostatic equilibrium dP/dr = -G M_r rho / r^2 by balancing forces on a thin shell, and write mass continuity dM_r/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho.
Estimate the central pressure and temperature of the Sun from scaling arguments with the mean density and mean molecular weight.
State the virial theorem 2K + U = 0 for a gravitating gas and show that a contracting star heats up while its total energy decreases (negative heat capacity).
Compute the Kelvin-Helmholtz timescale for the Sun and explain why gravitational contraction cannot power it for billions of years.

lessons.title: Equation of state: ideal gas, radiation, degeneracy
objectives: Write the ideal-gas pressure with mean molecular weight mu and compute mu for fully ionized hydrogen/helium/metals mixtures.
Write radiation pressure P_rad = aT^4/3 and find the temperature and mass regime where it rivals gas pressure.

Derive the scaling of electron degeneracy pressure, P proportional to rho^(5/3) nonrelativistic and rho^(4/3) relativistic, from the Pauli principle and the uncertainty relation (the free-electron gas of a metal).
Decide, for a given (rho, T), whether ideal gas, radiation, or degenerate-electron pressure dominates.

lessons.title: Nuclear fusion as the stellar energy source
objectives: Compute the energy released in 4 H -> He-4 from the mass defect and the fraction of rest mass converted (about 0.7%), and estimate the Sun's nuclear lifetime.

Explain why fusion needs quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier at about 10^7 K, and describe the Gamow peak as the product of the Boltzmann tail and the tunneling probability (compare an Arrhenius rate).
Describe the pp chain and the CNO cycle and compare their temperature sensitivities (roughly T^4 versus T^16 to T^20).
Explain what sets the lifetime of a star on the main sequence and why massive stars die young.

lessons.title: Energy transport, stellar models, and the main sequence
objectives: Distinguish radiative from convective energy transport and state the criterion for convective instability qualitatively.
Write the four equations of stellar structure (mass, hydrostatic equilibrium, energy generation, energy transport) with their boundary conditions.
Use homology and the radiative diffusion equation to derive the main-sequence scalings L proportional to M^3 (roughly) and a lifetime t proportional to M/L.
State the Vogt-Russell theorem and explain how a numerical integration (shooting) builds a stellar model.

units.title: Stellar evolution and compact objects
units.summary: From collapsing clouds to the main sequence, giants, white dwarfs, supernovae, neutron stars, and black holes, driven by degeneracy pressure and nuclear fuel exhaustion.

lessons.title: Star formation and post-main-sequence evolution
objectives: Derive the Jeans criterion for gravitational collapse of an isothermal cloud and estimate the Jeans mass of a molecular cloud.
Describe pre-main-sequence contraction qualitatively and why protostars start on the Hayashi track.
Trace the evolution of a 1 and a 10 solar-mass star across the HR diagram: main sequence, red giant branch, helium ignition, AGB or core collapse.
Use the main-sequence turnoff of a star cluster to estimate its age.

lessons.title: White dwarfs and the Chandrasekhar limit
objectives: Explain a white dwarf as a star supported by electron degeneracy pressure and compute its typical density and radius.
Derive the mass-radius relation R proportional to M^(-1/3) by balancing gravity against nonrelativistic degeneracy pressure.
Argue why relativistic degeneracy (P proportional to rho^(4/3)) gives a maximum mass near 1.4 solar masses, the Chandrasekhar limit.
Describe white-dwarf cooling and how an accreting white dwarf reaching the limit produces a Type Ia supernova.

lessons.title: Supernovae, neutron stars, pulsars, and black holes
objectives: Describe the stages of core-collapse in a massive star (iron core, photodisintegration, neutronization, bounce) and show that about 99% of the energy leaves as neutrinos using E ~ GM^2/R.
Classify supernovae (Type Ia, Ib/c, II) by spectra and progenitor.
Estimate neutron-star radius (about 10 km) and density from neutron degeneracy and compare with nuclear density.
Explain a pulsar as a rotating magnetized neutron star and estimate its surface magnetic field and age from the period P and period derivative.
Compute the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c^2 and state when a remnant becomes a black hole (set up for S3).

units.title: Galaxies and the distance ladder
units.summary: The Milky Way and other galaxies as dynamical systems: rotation curves reveal dark matter, and the cosmic distance ladder leads to Hubble's law.

lessons.title: Galaxies, rotation curves, and dark matter
objectives: Place galaxies on the Hubble sequence and describe the Milky Way's disk, bulge, and halo.
Derive the enclosed-mass relation M(<r) = v^2 r / G for circular orbits and estimate the Milky Way's mass from the Sun's orbital speed and distance.
Show that a Keplerian curve v proportional to r^(-1/2) is expected beyond the visible mass and explain what flat observed curves imply about a dark halo.
Describe the rungs of the distance ladder (parallax, Cepheid period-luminosity, Type Ia supernovae) and how errors propagate.
List independent lines of evidence for dark matter: cluster dynamics, gravitational lensing, and the Bullet Cluster.

units.title: The expanding universe and the Friedmann equations
units.summary: Homogeneous, isotropic expansion described by a scale factor; the Friedmann equation from Newtonian energy conservation and its GR form; model universes and the benchmark Lambda-CDM cosmology.

lessons.title: Hubble's law, redshift, and the Robertson-Walker metric
objectives: State the cosmological principle and what homogeneous and isotropic mean observationally.
Derive Hubble's law v = H0 d from uniform expansion r = a(t) x and identify H = adot/a.
Define comoving coordinates and the scale factor, and relate cosmological redshift to scale factor, 1 + z = a(t0)/a(t_e).
Write the Robertson-Walker metric with curvature k and compute proper distance to a comoving object.
Estimate the Hubble time and Hubble distance from H0 of about 70 km/s/Mpc.

lessons.title: The Friedmann equations
objectives: Derive the Friedmann equation from energy conservation for a test shell in an expanding uniform sphere and state its general-relativistic form with curvature.
Derive the fluid equation from the first law dE = -P dV applied to a comoving volume (adiabatic expansion of a gas of photons or dust) and state the acceleration equation.
Use P = w rho c^2 to show rho proportional to a^(-3(1+w)) for matter (w = 0), radiation (w = 1/3), and a cosmological constant (w = -1).
Compute the critical density rho_c = 3H^2/(8 pi G) and the density parameter Omega, and say what Omega > 1 and < 1 mean for curvature.

lessons.title: Model universes and the benchmark cosmology
objectives: Solve the Friedmann equation for single-component flat universes: a proportional to t^(2/3) for matter, t^(1/2) for radiation, e^(Ht) for Lambda.
Compute the age of a flat matter-only universe t0 = 2/(3 H0) and compare it with the Lambda-CDM age of about 13.8 Gyr.
Find the redshift of matter-radiation equality (about 3400) and describe when each component dominated.
Describe the benchmark model (Omega_m near 0.3, Omega_Lambda near 0.7, Omega_r about 10^-4) and classify possible fates of the universe.

units.title: Observational cosmology and the early universe
units.summary: Distances in an expanding universe, supernovae and dark energy, the CMB, Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and inflation.

lessons.title: Cosmic distances, supernovae, and dark energy
objectives: Define luminosity distance and angular-diameter distance in an expanding universe and explain why d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A.
Compute d_L for a flat matter-dominated universe at small z and show it reduces to cz/H0.
Explain how Type Ia supernovae as standard candles revealed cosmic acceleration and read Omega_Lambda off a magnitude-redshift diagram.
Compute the deceleration parameter q0 = Omega_m/2 - Omega_Lambda and interpret its sign.
Describe the cosmological constant as vacuum energy and state the size of the mismatch with the naive quantum-field estimate.

lessons.title: The cosmic microwave background
objectives: Show that blackbody radiation stays blackbody in an expanding universe with T proportional to 1/a, so T(z) = T0 (1+z) with T0 = 2.725 K.
Use the Saha equation for hydrogen to estimate why recombination happens near 3000 K (about 0.25 eV) rather than at 13.6 eV (an ionization equilibrium with a huge photon-to-baryon ratio).
Describe the CMB's measured properties: near-perfect Planck spectrum, dipole from our motion, and anisotropies at 10^-5.
Explain qualitatively how the acoustic peaks encode the geometry (first peak), baryon density, and dark-matter density.

lessons.title: Big Bang nucleosynthesis and inflation
objectives: Derive the neutron-to-proton ratio n/p = exp(-Q/kT) with Q = 1.29 MeV at freeze-out, and include neutron decay until deuterium forms.
Compute the primordial helium mass fraction Y_p = 2(n/p)/(1+n/p), about 0.25, and explain the deuterium bottleneck (a Saha-type equilibrium with a very small baryon-to-photon ratio).
State the flatness, horizon, and monopole problems of the hot Big Bang model.
Explain how a period of quasi-exponential expansion, a proportional to e^(Ht), solves them and estimate the roughly 60 e-folds required.
Describe slow-roll inflation with a scalar field and how quantum fluctuations seed density perturbations.
